content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper describes a metric to quantify the generalizability of trained CNNs, based on the idea that convolution kernels should be specific to certain features, and you want as many independent features as you want. This idea is quantified in the proposed Activation Representation Substitution metric. It consists of two steps, first for each kernel (or activation map) the input is optimized to maximize the response for that activation, whilst similtaneously minimizing the response in other layers. Here the idea is to obtain an input that is as specific as possible for that activation. Secondly, this input is provided to the network, and the response for all activations are measured. Ideally, only the corresponding activation would fire whereas the others shouldn't. If the others also fire this means that the kernel encodes for an unspecific feature and could in principle be substituted by the other hight activity kernels, the representations are said to be entangled.

In several experiments the authors show that the metric gives a good indication for the relevance of the seleted feature (removing these filters/activations drops performance). The metric is also compared to other approaches which confirms the intuition behind the metric. Finally, the metric is compared to the standard approach (testing on hold-out test set), where again their metric correlates well with good generalization capability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths and Weaknesses

The paper addresses an important problem and finds an interesting solution that seems to correlate well with generalization performance. Experimental results are promising.

Weaknesses
* My main concern with the paper is the lack of precision. At times the paper is hard to follow due to confusing, and seemlingly contradictory, sentences as well as some missing details. See comments below [B]
* From a practical point of view, it would have been nice to use the metric to do model selection. I believe the point of the paper is that the proposed MARS metric is a good proxy for generalization capability. What better way to show this to use it using hyperparameter sweeps or model design, and show that it is more reliable then the standard approach, which is e.g. model selection based on a validation set? 
* Some technical details are missing and some are not well motivated (see [A])

**[A] Comments on technical details**
1. A main concern that I have with the formulated objectives is that the argmax problem is probably ill-posed if no batch normalization is applied or if the input is not constraint to have a fixed norm. That is, if a conv layer response to some input then we could simply multiply that input by a large constant to increase the activation. And thus the argmax will never reach a (local) optimum and will keep ever increasing the magnitude of the input, without really channge the pattern that is supposed to be specific.
2. Another perhaps implicit assumption is that ReLU activation functions are used in the IAM object (eq 2). Here the activations are subtracted, but what if the outputs of h have negative values? Then the maximization strategy aims to make these values even more negative. Is this desirable?
3. For MARS per layer alpha parameter is specified. Why do we need such a hyperparameter, and why do we not just take the average over all layers. It is furthermore said that it should have a larger value for shallow layers, but lower for deeper. Why?
4. Below eq 4 "... denotes the dimension... " and "... N_{x_{l,i}} denotes the dimension of the output activation ...". What does it mean? The dimension of the feature maps is fixed right? Perhaps it represents a pixel count?
5. In the count of activations N_{x_{l,j}>x_{l,i}}, how is such a count achieved? Do you do pooling over the spatial domain? How is an activation even defined? I.e., the output of a layer is a whole feature map, which for every convolution kernel, or channel, has for every pixel an activation right? Then there needs to be some form of pooling. Is the great than condition applied before or after pooling?

**[B] Comments on readability**
1. It would have helped to have a precise definition of "entanglement". Especially the introduction was hard to read because also notion such as a "representation" was not defined yet. See e.g. "In this regard, we argue, ... between the representation of their main compoment of conovlution kernels" what is furthermore meant with "main component"?
2. Also: "When a convolution kernel has a low ARS, only a few other kernels are responsive to its representation". This sentence was also impossible to understand without first reading the paper. The word "representatin" could mean many things (e.g. a feature vector, or latent vector, the actual kernel, ...). Without a definition one cannot understand what it means for a kernel to "respond" to a representation.
3. In the methods section, the authors often talk about "continuously updated", perhaps a more accurate term would be "iteratively"; I don't understand which part about it is continuous.
4. "These convolution kernels are located on different convolution layers", what does it mean for a kernel to be "located" in a layer. The kernels define the layers...
5. "In the gradual update" -> "In the gradient update"?
6. "However, in CNNs, the representation of convolution kernels are entangled". Also here, I believe it would help a lot to make precise the notion of entanglement, which along the paper becomes clear but not upon first reading.
7. "However, because some representations of the convolution kernels are similar or meaningless, there could still be many convolution kernels that produce a high response in the same layer" This sentence is unclear. Is it meant that "... could be many representations of other convolution kernels that..."?
8. Last sentence of first paragraph of 2.2: "Representations are not substitutable, indicating that the model has more representations."? What does this mean? In the prior sentence it is mentioned that "we need to evaluate whether the representation of the convolution kernel can be substituted" and in the next paragraph you propose "Representational Substitution" which suggest that representation are substitutable? It is sentences like these that make the paper confusing. Are representations substitutable or not?
9. Start of 2.2: Suggested change: "After obtaining the disentangled representation" -> "After obtaining a maximally disentangled representation" since there is not one unique repr (so the -> a) and the reps are not purely disentangled, afterall the the IAM measures disentanglement on a continuous scale, right? What (2) does is trying to disentangle as good as possible.
10. After equation 3: "$x_{l,i}$ refers to the out activation of the target convolution kernel". This is confusing as before the symbol $x$ was used to refer to the (input) representation of a kernel, as obtained by the IAM, and now it refers to the output...
11. Section 2.3 starts with "However," words like However always respond to something written or said before, it is bad habit to start a paragraph with however.
12. In this same section the second "cause" can also be a bit better explained. Apparently "(2) the convolution kernels do not learn the features", what are "the features"?
13. Perhaps also because of the ambiguous writing, it is hard to understand the purpose of the experiments. The paper can be improved what answers are saught after with the experiments, and be explicit about whether or not these are confirmed.
14. Section 3.1. It is really hard to follow what the objective is of section 3.1. Am I correct to assume that its purpose is to validate the "independence" property stimulated by IAM? Be explicit about its purpose, and about the results/conclusions.
15. Section 3.2. What does "abblate" mean in this context. Apparently some convolutions can be "abblated", which means removed from the NN? How are they then removed? These are important details.
16. Section 3.4 is on CS. A bit more detail on what CS is would be appreciated in order to make the paper more self-contained.

The paper is experimentally of good quality and seems to comprise an appropriate set of experiments (though I think an important one generalization is missing, see my note on model selection). The work is novel and should be reproducible.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper works on the problem of the effectiveness of feature representations in convolutional neural networks. The major motivation is to examine the ``substitution'' of Conv. kernels by the iterative gradient method. Concretely, the method first computes an input that maximizes a kernel while suppressing the others. Then, the input is used to check how the targeted kernel responds to the input compared to the kernels that are suppressed. In the experimental analysis, the authors demonstrate the proposed metric is highly related to other metrics such as accuracy and class selectivity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The proposed metric seems to function well. If it is proven to also work in recent network structures with more varied tasks, it will be a popular choice for this community.

Weaknesses:

The major weakness of this paper is, there is no strong application connected with it. Although in section 3.2, the authors show that removing kernels with certain ARS scores will not hurt the performance, hence suggesting designing compression algorithms with it. But how effective it is in terms of compression compared to the existing compression algorithms? There is no discussion on this point.

At the end of section 3.3, the authors claim ``many of the convolution kernels are close to 1, which indicates that the model generalization ability is poorer'' and later in 3.4 ''ARS explains the conclusion of CS about the model's generalizability''. However, there is no strong clue that the distribution of ASR is related to the generalization ability, removing kernels with high ARS might not change the final classification results, but it may lower the classification confidence and robustness toward noisy samples, do we say the generalization ability will be the same?

The experimental configuration is slightly out-of-date, and I would like to see the authors provide results based on recent works.

Also, some of the claims in this paper are confusing. For instance, at the end of section 2.1, ``because some representations of the convolution kernels are similar or meaningless'', I somehow understand what is similar but how do you define ``meaningless''?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:

This paper is well-organized and provided a good overview of the proposed method, I have understood all the details I want to know about the ARS.

Quality:

The overall quality of this work is not satisfying because of the weaknesses mentioned.

Novelty:

The paper proposed a somewhat new method base on the former works, therefore the novelty is not that high.

Reproducibility:

I guess there should be no problem with reproducibility since the method is not very complicated.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, a metric Activation Representation Substitution is proposed that quantifies generalizability in deep neural networks.

The results show that if ARS is small for large number of convolutional filters , the model is more generalizable. This is shown through several experiments that also show that batch normalization leads to low ARS values thus better generalizability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. A new metric for generalizability is proposed that does not require any new data
2. Although experiments are done only on two models, the evaluation in different setting show promise of the proposed metric in quantifying generalizability
3. Innovative use of activation maximization. AM has been used in literature to inspect what a neuron encodes by visualizing maximally activating images for that neuron. This paper proposes a simple extension that allows quantification of how many neurons are encoding something relevant and not redundant. 

Weaknesses:
1. The writing is quite difficult to follow e.g. page 4 1st paragraph it took me multiple reads to follow what the authors are trying to say.
2.  The approach is compute inefficient. For each neuron, we need to do gradient descent and that can lead to large amount of GPU hours if one needs to probe large models.
3. The word "representation" means different thing to different people, here it is used in different context and can lead to confusion. I would recommend using something more specific to this paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Overall the paper is clear but it can be improved much more by simplifying the text and maybe a rewrite after a proofread.

Quality: The idea, results, experiments are of high quality. Writing however is not up to mark. I recommend authors to simplify some of the explanations and text that is unnecessary complicated.
 
Novelty: The idea to extend Activation maximization to quantify how many neurons are relevant and thus quantify generalizability is innovative and novel.

Reproducability: The idea is easy to implement, with existing implementations of AM already available in open source. I also recommend authors to release the code to reproduce at least a part of their experiment.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I find the idea quite interesting. The results present validate the proposed idea sufficiently. However, I believe the writing can be improved to better communicate the idea to general audience. 

Therefore, I recommend weak acceptance.

content.title: Exploring the Generalizability of CNNs via Activated Representational Substitution
content.TL;DR: We propose an metric named Activation Representation Substitution (ARS)  to explore the association between representations learned by convolution kernels and generalization.
content.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various fields due to their excellent generalizability. To explore the relationship between CNN representations and generalization, we propose an Activation Representation Substitution (ARS) metric based on the disentangled visual representations of convolution kernels. Without additional data, we obtain the disentangled visual representation of a kernel in the convolutional layer by iterating over a random image, and feed it into the CNN. The output activations of the other kernels in that convolutional layer are then investigated. When all other output activations are small, the ARS of the convolution kernel from that representation is also small, indicating that the representation is important for CNN. Our experiments with ablation analysis confirm the importance of the low ARS convolution kernel on accuracy. With ARS, we also explain batch normalization and class selectivity. By comparing the model performances on the test set, we empirically find that when the convolutional layer contains a large number of low ARS convolution kernels, the model has good generalization. ARS is a metric that can be used to better understand model generalizability without using external data.
